e.t: This Hebrew word refers to “strength”—the ability or power associated with a person, ruler, army, or God. It is used throughout the Old Testament, appearing 62 times, and can describe strength as something possessed, displayed, or attributed to the LORD. Its settings include speech about God’s greatness and accounts involving rulers and human capability. The surrounding verse determines whose strength is meant and how it is being considered.

This Hebrew word describes something being taken away or left spoiled. Its approved renderings include “away” and “spoiled,” showing a range centered on the removal or loss of something. It occurs 30 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so its basic sense appears in several kinds of passages rather than belonging to one narrow setting. The precise force in a particular verse depends on what is being removed, damaged, or lost there.

This Hebrew noun means “polls,” functioning as the term used when individuals are counted one by one. Its uses belong to Old Testament counting language, especially in Numbers, and it appears 12 times in the Hebrew corpus. The word occurs in lists and reckonings involving the people, so its normal sense is tied to counting each person individually rather than describing a general group. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding wording.

This word refers to “wings,” the body parts associated with flying or covering. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs three times, all in Daniel 7:4 and Daniel 7:6. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning remains straightforward: wings. The word is therefore a concrete noun describing a birdlike or winged feature rather than an action, quality, or abstract idea.

This Hebrew word describes being urged forward quickly—being “hasted” or “pressed.” It functions as an action word for moving or causing movement with urgency rather than delay. In its four Old Testament occurrences, it is rendered with these ideas in accounts from 2 Chronicles and Esther. The exact force can depend on the surrounding sentence: it may describe someone hurrying, or people being pressed onward. Its basic sense is rapid, urgent movement.

This Hebrew verb means “make,” expressing the action of bringing something about or causing it to be done. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Job 19:3. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the precise force of the word in that sentence cannot be described further. Its basic sense is an action—someone makes or causes something, rather than a person, object, or quality.

This Hebrew word centers on the idea of a “child.” It functions as a descriptive word in Old Testament sentences connected with pregnancy, birth, or a child’s presence, so its precise English wording depends on the sentence. It occurs 16 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, from Genesis through Amos. The repeated rendering “child” provides the clearest ordinary sense available here, while the surrounding verse determines how that sense is expressed.

This Hebrew noun means “husk,” referring to the outer covering of a seed or grain. It occurs once in the Hebrew Bible, so its normal meaning is represented by a single usage rather than a broad range of passages. The word appears in Numbers 6:4. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding context, but the word itself identifies a husk or outer covering.

e.t: This Hebrew word is a personal name, rendered “Haggith.” It identifies a particular woman rather than expressing a general quality, action, or object. The name appears five times in the Old Testament, in passages that refer to her in connection with David’s family. Because it functions as a proper name, its meaning is primarily identification: it tells the reader who is being referred to, not what that person is like. Its precise significance in any individual passage depends on the surrounding verse and narrative context.

This Hebrew word is a distinct lexical term, but its ordinary meaning cannot be stated securely from the preserved information. It appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, at Ezekiel 27:18, and no explicit definition, gloss, or approved meaning term is available. The reference identifies where the word occurs, but without the verse text it does not establish what the word describes or how it functions there. Its precise sense therefore requires the surrounding passage and direct contextual evidence.

This Hebrew word means “power.” It is a noun naming power as something a person or ruler may possess or exercise. In the Hebrew corpus, it occurs twice, both in Daniel. Its precise role in either verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central sense remains power itself rather than an action or command. The word appears in Daniel 2:37 and Daniel 4:30, with the same basic meaning in each occurrence.

Huppah is a Hebrew personal name, rendered as “Huppah.” It functions as a name rather than as a general word describing an object, action, or quality. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 24:13. Because the available information identifies the name but does not include the verse text or surrounding passage, its particular role in that list cannot be explained further here.

This Hebrew verb means “hold.” It describes the action of holding something or someone. In its Old Testament use, the basic idea is an active act of holding rather than merely seeing or having. The word occurs 67 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so it serves in several kinds of sentences while retaining this central sense. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

This Hebrew word means “taste.” It functions as a noun, naming taste or what is experienced through tasting. The word can also serve in sentences where taste is used figuratively, so the surrounding context determines its precise force. It occurs 12 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including passages involving food and passages describing human conduct or understanding. Its central idea remains taste, whether used physically or in a broader figurative way.

This Hebrew word expresses the action or request to “Give.” It commonly functions as a direct appeal or command, calling someone to provide or hand something over. It occurs 33 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so its basic sense is established across a range of passages rather than being limited to one setting. The surrounding words determine what is to be given and to whom, but the word itself centers on giving.

This Hebrew word refers to Greek people, or people associated with Greece. It is a national or ethnic designation rather than a description of an action, quality, or object. The word appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Joel 4:6. Its precise significance in that verse must be understood from the surrounding passage, but its basic reference is to Greeks as a people. The Hebrew lemma identifies this word as יְוָנִי, a term connected with Greece and its inhabitants.

This Hebrew verb expresses that something is good, turns out well, or is favorably regarded. It can describe a condition, outcome, or response, and it may be rendered “said” when someone speaks favorably or agrees with something. The word occurs 112 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so its basic idea appears across many settings rather than belonging to one narrow subject. Its precise sense in a particular verse depends on what is being described or affirmed.

It occurs five times in the Hebrew Old Testament, each in a different verse, including Deuteronomy 11:10, 1 Kings 21:2, Proverbs 15:17, and Isaiah 37:27. Its precise significance in any one verse depends on that passage’s surrounding wording.

This Hebrew word means “burning.” It identifies the idea of burning rather than describing a broader set of meanings. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 3:24. Since the word appears only there and the surrounding verse text is not available here, its precise role in that sentence must be understood from the context. Its basic meaning remains “burning.”

This Hebrew word means “villages.” It is a plural noun used to name more than one village. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in 1 Chronicles and once in Song of Songs. The available rendering identifies the same meaning each time, while the surrounding verse text is not provided here, so the word’s specific force in either passage cannot be described further. Its central sense remains a reference to villages.

The word’s basic sense is therefore concrete and straightforward, while its precise force in that sentence depends on the surrounding passage. Its single occurrence does not establish a broader range of meanings within the Hebrew Old Testament.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to a dowry—the gift or payment associated with arranging a marriage. It functions as a noun for something given in connection with a woman’s marriage, and its scriptural uses occur in passages involving discussion or giving. The word appears three times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including Genesis 34:12, Exodus 22:17, and 1 Samuel 18:25. Its central meaning is “dowry.”

This Hebrew word expresses the action of striking or smiting—hitting with force. It occurs four times in the Old Testament, appearing in Ezra and Daniel. The approved English meanings are “smote” and “struck,” showing that it normally functions as an action word describing a forceful blow or impact. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic sense is direct physical striking rather than a broad description of harm or defeat.

This Hebrew word refers to “ears,” the organs used for hearing. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Deuteronomy 23:25. As a concrete bodily term, its basic meaning is direct and specific rather than abstract: it identifies ears as part of the human body. The surrounding verse determines what action involving the ears is being described, but the word itself carries the ordinary meaning “ears.”

e.t: This Hebrew noun refers to a “portion,” an amount or piece assigned, given, or designated for someone. It is used for portions connected with offerings, meals, and gifts, and can also identify something appointed for a person. The word occurs 14 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing a consistent idea of an allotted portion rather than an action or quality. Its surrounding context determines what is being apportioned.

This Hebrew word functions as “it,” pointing to something already identified in the sentence and serving as the object of an action or description. In the Hebrew Old Testament data, it occurs twice, in 1 Kings 6:7 and Job 41:26. Since no fuller definition is available here, its precise referent must be determined from the surrounding words in each passage. Thus, the word’s normal function is to refer back to an already mentioned thing.

This word means “that” and functions as a connective, joining one statement to another clause. It commonly helps introduce what is being said, intended, or brought about, while its exact force depends on the sentence around it. It appears 272 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so it is a broadly used linking word rather than a term limited to one subject or setting.

This Hebrew word refers to a “burden”—something carried or borne. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Isaiah 30:27. Its ordinary sense is the idea of a burden or load. It functions as a term naming what is borne, rather than an action or quality. The surrounding passage determines the precise force of the word in that occurrence.

The Hebrew word means “stay,” referring to something that provides support or steadiness. It functions as a term for dependable support rather than an action. In the Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs five times in three verses: 2 Samuel 22:19, Psalm 18:18, and Isaiah 3:1. Its repeated use in Isaiah shows that the word can describe support regarded as essential; the exact force in any verse depends on its surrounding wording.

This Hebrew noun refers to “sheepfolds,” places where sheep are kept. It appears twice in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, in Genesis 49:14 and Judges 5:16. Its basic use is concrete and ordinary: it identifies the enclosures associated with sheep rather than describing a person, action, or quality. The surrounding wording determines how the noun functions in each verse, but its central reference remains sheepfolds.

The word means “thousand,” referring to the number 1,000. It is used in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus for large numerical totals, rather than as a description of a person, object, or action. This word occurs five times, all in Daniel, in two verses. Its normal sense is therefore straightforward: it identifies a group or amount numbering one thousand. The surrounding wording determines what is being counted in any particular verse.

This Hebrew noun refers to the nostrils—the openings of the nose. It names a bodily feature rather than an action or quality. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, at Job 41:20, so its ordinary sense is supported by that straightforward rendering and should be understood as a simple body-part term. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain its particular use there.

e.t: This Hebrew word identifies someone who is “young.” It functions as a noun referring to a young person rather than expressing an action or command. The word appears 76 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so it is a regularly used term for describing age or youth. Its precise reference—whether to a particular individual or to young people generally—depends on the sentence and surrounding passage. It occurs in narratives, laws, and family-related passages.

This Hebrew word refers to something “mouldy.” It is used for a food item rather than for an action, person, or place. The word appears three times in the Hebrew Old Testament: twice in Joshua and once in 1 Kings. In each occurrence, it identifies food in a deteriorated or stale condition. Its central meaning is therefore a description of mouldiness in something prepared as food, with the surrounding verse determining the exact item being described.

The word means “burn” and functions as a verb, describing an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs three times, appearing once each in Psalms, Isaiah, and Ezekiel. Its recorded uses are found at Psalm 78:21, Isaiah 44:15, and Ezekiel 39:9. The precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This word is a personal name, not a general term describing an action, quality, or object. It appears twice in the Hebrew text, both times in Daniel 1:7. The available record does not provide a short definition or approved meaning term for the name, so its ordinary lexical sense cannot be stated more specifically without adding information beyond the supplied Scripture evidence. Its use is connected with another name through the wording of that verse.

This Hebrew word means “made.” As a verb, it expresses an action performed by someone or something and identifies what that action does in a sentence. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Habakkuk 3:9. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, this entry gives the word’s basic lexical sense, while the exact force of the action must be understood from its sentence.

This Hebrew word means “help,” describing assistance or support given to someone. It commonly functions as an action—someone helps, strengthens, or comes to another’s aid—rather than naming a person or object. Its range includes human assistance and help attributed to God, so the surrounding sentence identifies who gives the help and who receives it. The word occurs 82 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing that helping is a recurring scriptural action from Genesis through Zechariah.

e.t: This Hebrew word is the personal name “Eli,” identifying a particular man rather than describing an action, quality, or relationship. It functions as a proper name in the Old Testament and is rendered consistently as “Eli.” It occurs 33 times in 30 verses, appearing chiefly in 1 Samuel and once in 1 Kings. The name’s precise significance in any passage comes from the surrounding verse and narrative.

This Hebrew word expresses something deep or profound. It can describe physical depth, as well as something hidden, difficult to reach, or penetrating in character. In the Old Testament, it occurs nine times, all in the Hebrew Bible corpus, and its dominant sense is “deep.” The word may therefore point to depth in a place, a matter concealed from view, or an action that reaches deeply. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

The Hebrew word means “shut.” It describes something as shut and functions in a sentence to state that condition or action.
